title: Bibim Guksu
subtitle: Spicy cold mixed noodles
excerpt: Bibim guksu is a Korean cold noodle dish in which thin noodles are tossed in a bold gochujang sauce and topped with cucumber, kimchi, and a hard-boiled egg. It serves 2 and is ready in 20 minutes. The combination of cold noodles, hot sauce, and sharp toppings makes it one of the most refreshing Korean meals in summer.
sourceNotes: Bibim guksu is a summer dish with roots in Korean home cooking traditions that valued cool, refreshing noodle dishes during the hottest months. The word bibim refers to the act of mixing and appears in several Korean dish names including bibimbap. Cold noodle dishes have been part of Korean eating culture for centuries, with regional variations across the peninsula.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce can be made up to 3 days ahead and stored in the fridge. Cook the noodles and assemble just before eating.

glossaryTerms.definition: Bibim is a Korean term meaning mixed or to mix. It appears in the names of several dishes where the key action is tossing all components together at the table or in the bowl before eating. Bibimbap (mixed rice), bibim guksu (mixed noodles), and bibim naengmyeon (mixed cold noodles) all share this mixing principle at their core.

Guksu is the Korean word for noodles, particularly thin wheat noodles. It also refers to dishes in which these noodles are the central ingredient. Guksu appears in both hot soup-based dishes and cold mixed preparations, and the term is used interchangeably with myeon in some regional dialects.

content.text: This recipe serves 2 and takes 20 minutes. Bibim
is a cold Korean noodle dish where the

action of tossing everything together is part of the experience. Thin noodles are cooked, chilled under cold water, and then mixed in a gochujang-based sauce with cucumber, kimchi, and spring onions. A hard-boiled egg halved on top finishes the bowl.

Rinsing the noodles under cold running water immediately after cooking is non-negotiable for this dish. It stops the cooking, removes excess starch, and cools the noodles so they do not clump. Shake them dry before adding the sauce, otherwise the water dilutes the dressing. The sauce should be assertively flavoured: it will mellow when tossed with the noodles and toppings.
Bring a pot of water to the boil. Cook the noodles according to the packet instructions, usually 4 to 6 minutes. Drain and rinse immediately under cold running water. Shake dry and set aside.
Mix together the gochujang, sesame oil, rice vinegar, sugar, and garlic in a large bowl to make the sauce.
Add the noodles to the bowl and toss with the sauce until evenly coated.
Divide the noodles between two bowls. Top each with the cucumber, kimchi, and a halved hard-boiled egg.
Scatter over the spring onions and sesame seeds. Serve immediately.

items.cause: They were not rinsed thoroughly or were left too long before saucing
items.fix: Rinse the noodles under cold water for at least 30 seconds, tossing them as you rinse. Toss with a few drops of sesame oil immediately after draining if not saucing straight away

items.symptom: The sauce is too thick to coat the noodles evenly
items.cause: Gochujang varies in thickness between brands
items.fix: Add a teaspoon of water to the sauce and stir until it loosens to a consistency that coats a spoon smoothly

items.symptom: The dish is not spicy enough
items.cause: Gochujang varies in heat and some brands are quite mild
items.fix: Add half a teaspoon of gochugaru to the sauce and mix well. Start with a small amount and adjust to taste before tossing with the noodles

content.text: Bibim guksu is a summer lunch dish in Korea. It is eaten on hot days when a warming soup or stew feels like too much effort, and the cold, spicy noodles provide immediate relief. It is also a quick midweek meal that comes together from pantry ingredients once the sauce components are at hand. Korean households keep gochujang in the fridge as a constant, so this dish can be made on very short notice. The toppings vary by what is available: cucumber is standard, kimchi and egg are very common, and some versions include thin strips of perilla leaf or a splash of fruit vinegar in the sauce.
